why: Application support and data engineering jobs run on Linux servers. Interviews often ask you to find something in a log from the command line.
outcome: navigate a server, read and search files and logs, check processes and disk, and write a small Bash script.

lessons.title: Navigate and manage files
text: Everything is a file in a tree starting at /. Your shell has a current directory; commands act relative to it unless you give an absolute path.
Permissions say who can read (r), write (w) and execute (x) a file: the owner, the group, everyone else.
points: pwd, ls -lah, cd, mkdir -p, cp, mv, rm (no undo).
~ is your home directory; . is here; .. is the parent.
chmod +x script.sh makes a script executable; chown changes the owner.
Tab completes names; the up arrow recalls commands; Ctrl+C stops a command.

example.code:
cd /var/log/myapp
ls -lah            # sizes and dates
mkdir -p ~/backup/2026-10
cp app.log ~/backup/2026-10/
chmod 640 ~/backup/2026-10/app.log

lessons.title: Read and search logs
text: Most investigations are: find the time of the problem, find the error lines, read the context around them.
Commands combine with the pipe |: the output of one becomes the input of the next.
points: less file (search with /text, quit with q); tail -n 100 file; tail -f file to follow live.
grep -i "error" file, grep -n for line numbers, grep -C 5 for 5 lines of context.
grep -c counts matches; sort | uniq -c | sort -nr counts distinct lines.

example.code:
# errors in the last 1000 lines, with context
tail -n 1000 app.log | grep -i -C 3 "error"

# most frequent error messages today
grep "2026-10-29" app.log | grep ERROR | cut -d' ' -f4- | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head

lessons.title: Processes, disk, network and scripts
text: When an application is slow or down, check if the process runs, how much CPU and memory it uses, whether the disk is full, and whether the port answers.
A Bash script saves a sequence of commands. Start it with a shebang and make it stop on errors.
points: ps aux | grep java; top or htop for live usage; kill <pid> (kill -9 only as last resort).
df -h for disk space; du -sh * | sort -h to find big folders; free -h for memory.
systemctl status myapp; journalctl -u myapp --since "1 hour ago".
curl -I http://localhost:8080/health checks an HTTP endpoint; ss -tlnp lists listening ports.
set -euo pipefail at the top of a script stops on the first error.

example.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
# health.sh: quick health check for an app
APP=myapp
systemctl is-active --quiet "$APP" && echo "$APP running" || echo "$APP DOWN"
df -h / | tail -1
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "health: %{http_code}\n" http://localhost:8080/health

lessons.title: Users, permissions and SSH
text: Every file has an owner, a group and three sets of permissions: read (r), write (w) and execute (x) for the owner, the group and everyone else. Many 'it does not work on the server' problems are permission problems: the app user cannot read its config or write its log folder.

SSH is how you reach servers. Use key pairs instead of passwords: the private key stays on your machine, the public key goes on the server in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. sudo runs one command as root when you really need it.
points: chmod 640 file: owner read+write, group read, others nothing (r=4, w=2, x=1).
chown user:group changes the owner; -R applies to a whole folder.
Never chmod 777 to 'fix' a problem: find which user needs which access.
~/.ssh/config stores host aliases, users and keys so ssh prod is enough.

example.code:
ls -l deploy.sh
# -rw-r--r-- 1 anna devops 812 Oct 30 09:12 deploy.sh
chmod u+x deploy.sh            # owner can execute
sudo chown app:app /srv/app -R  # give the folder to the app user

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "anna@laptop"
ssh-copy-id anna@server.example.com
ssh anna@server.example.com 'df -h /'
scp report.csv anna@server.example.com:/tmp/
example.note: Keep private keys private (chmod 600) and protect them with a passphrase.

items: Go back to the previous directory
Logs changed in the last day

pitfalls: rm -rf with a variable that turns out empty: always quote variables and double-check paths.
Restarting a service before saving the logs that explain the crash.
Using kill -9 first: the process cannot clean up.
Scripts without set -e that keep going after a failed step.

exercises.q: Show the 20 most recent lines that contain 'ERROR' or 'FATAL' in app.log.
The disk is full. Find the 10 biggest folders under /var.
Count requests per HTTP status code in an access log where the status is the 9th field.
Make /srv/app/backup.sh executable by its owner and group only, readable by the group, invisible to others, owned by user backup and group ops.

interview.q: An application is slow. What do you check on the server?
interview.a: Is the process up (systemctl / ps)? CPU and memory (top), disk space and I/O (df -h, iostat), recent errors in logs (tail, grep), dependencies such as the database and network (curl, ping), and what changed recently (deployments, config).
Owner can read, write, execute (7); group and others can read and execute (5). Typical for scripts and directories.

interview.q: How do you follow a log in real time and only see errors?
An application cannot write its log file after a deployment. How do you investigate?
interview.a: Check which user the process runs as (ps -o user= -p PID or the service file), then ls -l on the log file and its folder to see owner, group and permissions, and whether the disk is full (df -h) or the filesystem read-only. Fix the ownership or permissions for that user specifically with chown or chmod, never with 777, and add it to the deployment so it does not come back.
